blocks.heading: Choosing an appropriate form
blocks.text: Choose ownership by matching the arrangement to the circumstances. A sole trader may suit a modest owner-managed activity requiring quick decisions and little finance. A partnership can pool skills and money when partners can agree on decisions and profit sharing. A private limited company may suit a group seeking continuity and limited liability while retaining a restricted ownership circle; a public limited company may suit much wider equity funding when owners accept wider participation and scrutiny. A co-operative fits members seeking a shared benefit and democratic influence. A close corporation can suit a small group wanting incorporated ownership with member involvement. A public corporation may fit a state service objective. A joint venture can combine complementary resources for a specific project, whereas a franchise can provide an established brand and business format in exchange for fees and restrictions. Compare actual advantages and costs rather than ranking forms universally. Availability of finance, willingness to share control, liability, purpose, continuity and the owners’ skills can point in different directions. A supported decision identifies which constraint is decisive and states when an alternative would be preferable.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Fictional Sera Foods needs another owner’s investment for new ovens. Its founder wants to retain a small ownership group, and both investors are concerned about their personal exposure to business debt. Assume no personal guarantees are required. A private limited company meets the stated preference for a restricted ownership group and normally limited shareholder liability better than an ordinary partnership. It brings administration and shared decisions, so it is worthwhile only if the investment and risk benefits justify those costs. A public limited company would invite wider ownership than the founder currently wants. On these facts choose the private limited form, while recognising that a very small, low-risk start could have remained sole owned.
